How to submit music to community radio stations

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 3 min read Station-type submission guides

On this page
  • How community radio programming works
  • Which releases are a realistic fit?
  • Find the right submission contact
  • What to put in the pitch
  • A safe campaign workflow
  • Pre-send checklist

Community radio is one of the most reachable broadcast paths for independent artists because programming is local, eclectic, and frequently chosen by volunteer hosts. That openness is not a license to mass-email the staff list: the winning unit is a release matched to a specific show and a current submission route.

How community radio programming works

Most community stations combine a small permanent staff with volunteer presenters. A music director may screen general releases, while specialty hosts select every track for their own programs. Schedules can span dozens of genres, so a station-level label tells you less than a show playlist.

Community broadcasters are mission-led and accountable to listeners. Local culture, underrepresented music, public service, and participation often matter alongside sound. A truthful local or tour connection can therefore be more useful than streaming numbers.

Which releases are a realistic fit?

  • Local and regional releases with a clear community connection
  • Niche genres served by a named specialty program
  • Independent music that complements recent public playlists
  • Artists available for a concise interview, station ID, or local session

A station type is only the first filter. Confirm the format, recent playlist, service area, and individual show before collecting a contact. A relevant list of 40 prospects is a stronger campaign asset than 4,000 addresses selected only because they contain the word “radio.”

Find the right submission contact

For general rotation, the music director is usually the best first contact. For a narrowly defined style, a specialty-show host may be more relevant. Volunteer schedules change, making role and date verification essential.

  1. Read the station's current music or submission page and follow it over any general advice.
  2. Check the schedule and recent playlists for the show or format that matches the release.
  3. Confirm the named person still holds the role on the station's own site.
  4. Record the source URL and date checked beside the contact, so your list can be maintained.

What to put in the pitch

Name the show or recent playlist that establishes fit. Mention a genuine geographic connection where one exists and offer an interview or station ID only if you can deliver it promptly.

  • A specific subject line: artist, track, genre, release date
  • One sentence showing why this station or show is relevant
  • One stable streaming link, with a clean edit available where needed
  • Your city and any truthful local, tour, or audience connection
  • A direct ask to consider the track, followed by a polite sign-off

Use the radio pitch email templates as a framework, then rewrite the opening for every recipient.

A safe campaign workflow

Work in small waves. Research ten to twenty stations, send individual messages, then review replies and bounces before expanding. Suppress opt-outs immediately. Never scrape personal addresses, conceal the sender, or imply a prior relationship. Relevant one-to-one outreach protects your reputation and produces better learning than an indiscriminate blast.

Track public playlists, show archives, replies, and interview invitations. Small community spins can become durable relationships; a short thank-you after verified support is more valuable than another promotional blast.

Pre-send checklist

  • The station and show still operate, and the page was checked recently.
  • The release appears next to plausible peers in the current programming.
  • The recipient's role is relevant to music selection.
  • The email identifies you, contains an accurate subject, and offers an easy opt-out.
  • The campaign log has fields for sent date, response, follow-up, spin, and suppression.

Frequently asked questions

Do community radio stations accept independent music?

Many do, but each station and show sets its own process. Some use a central music director; others ask artists to contact a program directly. Check the official site immediately before sending.

Who should I contact at a community radio station?

Start with the named music director or genre show host. Use a dedicated submissions address when the station publishes one; do not bypass it by guessing personal addresses.

How often should I follow up?

Follow up once, seven to ten days after the first message, unless the station publishes a different process. Do not add the address to an automated sequence. If there is no reply after one relevant follow-up, record the outcome and move on.
